title: Isolation Levels Through Two-Connection Experiments
description: Compare READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE using reproducible snapshot, phantom, locking-read and write-skew experiments with solutions.

questions.question_text: What does a SQL isolation level help define?
options: Permitted interactions and observations between concurrent transactions
Whether all queries use one physical connection
questions.explanation: Isolation constrains concurrent behavior, while other correctness boundaries remain separate.

questions.question_text: Which lab setup is necessary for an interleaving experiment?
options: Two aliases in one SELECT only
questions.explanation: Separate connections allow one transaction to remain open while another acts.

questions.question_text: When should the lab choose the next transaction isolation level?
questions.explanation: The transaction context must have the intended setting when it begins.

questions.question_text: At READ COMMITTED, what snapshot do ordinary consistent reads generally use?
options: A fresh committed snapshot per statement
questions.explanation: A later statement may observe a transaction committed since the previous statement.

questions.question_text: B commits a change between A reads under READ COMMITTED. What can occur?
options: A missing primary key by definition
questions.explanation: The new observation is committed but differs from A’s earlier observation.

questions.question_text: What usually establishes an InnoDB REPEATABLE READ consistent-read snapshot?
options: The name of the transaction variable
The first ordinary consistent read in the transaction
questions.explanation: With ordinary transaction start semantics, first consistent-read timing matters.

questions.question_text: Can a REPEATABLE READ transaction observe its own writes?
questions.explanation: Own changes are visible even though other consistent reads use a snapshot.

questions.question_text: What distinguishes a locking read from an ordinary snapshot read?
options: It requests relevant locks and uses current-read behavior
questions.explanation: The two operations need separate visibility and blocking reasoning.

questions.question_text: What is a phantom observation about?
options: Changes to rows satisfying a predicate across observations
questions.explanation: Predicate membership is the relevant observation, rather than only one row value.

questions.question_text: Does a stable snapshot prove that the SELECT locked every matching gap?
options: Only when the result is empty
questions.explanation: Version visibility can preserve results without the locking behavior of a range locking read.

questions.question_text: What makes a dirty read dirty?
options: It later rolled back in every case
The observed change was uncommitted at observation time
The value was a negative integer
It came from a large table
questions.explanation: A later commit does not retroactively make the earlier uncommitted observation clean.

questions.question_text: Does READ UNCOMMITTED eliminate all write locking?
options: Only when a primary key exists
questions.explanation: Relaxed read visibility is not freedom from write conflicts or deadlocks.

questions.question_text: Two on-call workers each leave after observing the other. What rule is endangered?
options: Every row must have a different alias
The database must contain exactly two indexes
At least one worker must remain on call
questions.explanation: The cross-row invariant can fail even when the transactions write different rows.

questions.question_text: What makes a guard-row solution work?
options: Every relevant decision path locks the same guard before checking the invariant
Only one path knows the guard exists
The guard is read after commit
The guard has a decorative name
questions.explanation: Coordination requires universal participation by paths enforcing the shared rule.

questions.question_text: What does serializable execution aim to provide?
options: Results equivalent to some serial execution within its supported model
questions.explanation: Serial equivalence describes transaction results, not every application reliability concern.

questions.question_text: What must be considered when an engine reports a retryable serialization failure?
options: Repeat the complete logical transaction under a bounded policy
questions.explanation: Earlier observations and writes may no longer form a valid attempt.

questions.question_text: Why can session-level isolation changes matter to pooled connections?
options: They automatically clear all locks forever
They disable prepared statements by definition
Later borrowers may inherit changed session state
questions.explanation: Session defaults persist beyond one application request unless deliberately managed.

questions.question_text: B rolls back an update before A reads at READ COMMITTED. Which value should A avoid?
options: Every value from the primary key
questions.explanation: The stronger-level read does not expose B’s uncommitted version.

questions.question_text: Which observation depends on index and predicate details?
options: The spelling of the isolation keyword
The footprint of a locking range scan
questions.explanation: Different access paths can protect different records and intervals.

questions.question_text: What does one SQLite result fixture establish for this lab?
options: A limited query result, not InnoDB concurrency behavior
questions.explanation: Concurrency and engine-specific visibility need their own execution evidence.

notes:
## Ask which observations a transaction may make

An isolation level defines part of the contract between concurrent transactions. It tells you which interactions a database permits and which observations require stronger coordination. It is not a promise that every operation physically runs alone. A reporting query can read a consistent historical view while another transaction changes current rows. Conversely, a locking operation can inspect current records and wait even when an earlier ordinary read used a snapshot.

Consider an equipment desk with two cameras available. One transaction prepares a report while another allocates a camera. Should the report repeat its original observation, show the newest committed count on each statement, or coordinate with the allocation decision? Each purpose can require a different contract. Start with the required business invariant, then identify the reads, writes and predicates that must participate in its enforcement.

## Use a fixture with explicit connection boundaries

The following table is a synthetic local lab, not a production inventory. Run setup once and use two independent database connections called A and B. Confirm that the table uses InnoDB and that the statements are actually inside the intended transactions. Do not assume that two editor tabs share different connections or that a connection pool preserves session settings between unrelated requests.

```sql
CREATE TABLE isolation_lab (
  asset_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  available INT NOT NULL,
  category VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
INSERT INTO isolation_lab VALUES (1,2,'camera'),(2,4,'tripod');
```

Set the isolation level before the transaction begins. A bare SET TRANSACTION applies to the next transaction, while SET SESSION changes the default for subsequent transactions on that connection. Record the setting in the lab transcript. Returning a connection with changed session state to a pool can affect later requests, so real applications need deliberate initialization and cleanup rather than an untracked session command.

## Observe READ COMMITTED across two statements

Connection A starts at READ COMMITTED and reads the available value for asset one. Connection B then updates that row to one and commits. A reads again without ending its transaction. For these ordinary consistent reads, A should first see two and then one because each statement gets a fresh committed snapshot. B's uncommitted change must not be mistaken for the reason the second observation changed.

```sql
-- A
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT available FROM isolation_lab WHERE asset_id=1;
-- B executes and commits between A's reads
UPDATE isolation_lab SET available=1 WHERE asset_id=1;
-- A, after B has committed
SELECT available FROM isolation_lab WHERE asset_id=1;
COMMIT;
```

The B update above assumes its connection uses autocommit; alternatively write an explicit transaction and COMMIT there. A non-repeatable read means A observed different committed versions of the same row across statements. It is not a dirty read, because the intervening value was committed before the later statement. If this is an acceptable fresh dashboard observation, the changing result may be intentional rather than a defect.

## Repeat the experiment under REPEATABLE READ

Reset the fixture to two available cameras. At InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, A's first ordinary consistent read establishes the snapshot used by later consistent reads in that transaction. If B commits a change afterward, A's second such read still sees two. Starting a transaction alone does not necessarily establish this snapshot; the timing of the first consistent read matters for the usual START TRANSACTION behavior.

That repeatability does not mean the transaction sees only its initial snapshot under every statement. A sees its own changes, and locking reads operate differently from ordinary consistent reads. A FOR UPDATE lookup can observe a newer committed version while an ordinary read continues to use its earlier snapshot. Mixing these observations without understanding their roles can produce a mental model that no single real database state satisfies.

| Experiment | READ COMMITTED ordinary reads | REPEATABLE READ ordinary reads |
|---|---|---|
| B commits between A's two reads | Later statement can see the new value | Existing snapshot normally retains the old value |
| B changes but has not committed | New uncommitted version is not read | New uncommitted version is not read |
| A writes its own row | Own changes are visible | Own changes are visible |

## Distinguish snapshot stability from predicate protection

A phantom concerns a changed set of rows satisfying a predicate, such as additional available cameras appearing between observations. Under READ COMMITTED, later statements may see newly committed matching rows. Under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, ordinary snapshot reads can repeat their earlier set. That result follows from version visibility; it should not be explained as proof that every ordinary SELECT has locked every matching gap.

Locking range scans at REPEATABLE READ commonly use next-key protection that can prevent relevant inserts. The exact footprint depends on indexes, predicates and execution plans. A complete unique-key lookup, a range scan and an unsuccessful search are different cases. Consult the [locking protocol lab](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/locking-protocol-lab) for record and gap reasoning instead of treating the word phantom as a universal lock instruction.

## Write skew requires an invariant-level argument

Suppose two coordinators are both marked on call and the rule requires at least one to remain. Each transaction reads that another coordinator is available, then updates only its own row to off call. Snapshot repeatability alone does not establish that this cross-row rule survives concurrent decisions. The transactions can write different rows, so reasoning only about two writers touching the same row misses the invariant.

One design serializes decisions through an agreed guard row that every relevant path locks before checking availability. Another uses an appropriately verified serializable execution strategy with complete-transaction retries. The choice depends on actual engine semantics and access paths. A SELECT COUNT followed by an unrelated write is not automatically protected because both statements appear between START TRANSACTION and COMMIT.

## Understand the ends of the isolation spectrum

READ UNCOMMITTED permits observations that stronger levels exclude, including dirty reads. A dirty value may later commit or roll back; the defining feature is that it was uncommitted when observed. Lower isolation does not eliminate write locks or guarantee freedom from deadlocks. Benchmarking a read-heavy workload cannot establish correctness for a reservation workflow with concurrent writes.

SERIALIZABLE aims for results equivalent to some serial execution within its supported model. InnoDB can convert ordinary reads to shared locking reads when autocommit is disabled, producing blocking behavior unlike an unrestricted snapshot. Exact behavior depends on transaction context. Serializable does not solve application authorization, external side effects or request duplication. It can require retries and can change latency, so test both correctness and operational behavior.

## Keep a precise observation transcript

For each experimental step, record which connection executed the statement and whether that connection had an open transaction. Record the initial committed fixture, the first read that established a snapshot, each write and the commit or rollback that made the change visible. A result without this ordering information is ambiguous: the same query can legitimately produce different values under different interleavings. Avoid timing the experiment with a short sleep and hoping the intended order occurred. Explicit checkpoints between operators make the explanation reproducible.

Include missing-row and newly inserted-row variants. An existing primary-key lookup demonstrates one record, while checking that no matching reservation exists raises a predicate-level problem. A uniqueness constraint can arbitrate competing inserts for one defined key, but it cannot invent a cross-row capacity rule that the schema does not express. Explain exactly which invariant is enforced by a constraint and which remains the responsibility of the transaction protocol.

Also distinguish a slow query from a blocked query. Waiting for a conflicting transaction can dominate latency even when the lookup itself is efficient. Inspect the active transactions and their lock relationships before blaming the isolation level or adding an index. A performance change is acceptable only after rerunning the success, denial and rollback schedules that establish the business behavior.

## Solve and record two concurrency exercises

First exercise: under each of READ COMMITTED and REPEATABLE READ, schedule B's commit before and after A's first consistent read. Predict both A observations. The solution hinges on when the snapshot is established and whether the next statement gets a fresh snapshot. Include a version where B rolls back; its uncommitted replacement must not appear in the stronger-level ordinary reads. Reset fixture values between runs so one experiment does not accidentally supply another's initial state.

Second exercise: implement the on-call decision with two independent connections and an agreed guard lock. The solution requires every path to acquire the same guard before reading the shared invariant and deciding whether to leave. Verify one allowed departure, one denied departure and a rollback after the check. Record final rows, waits and any retryable errors. Single-session results and SQLite subset tests do not verify this InnoDB concurrency contract; see [isolation](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/isolation) and [lost updates](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/lost-update) for complementary failure patterns.
